subject: Throughput sizing & SLO follow-up (Finex)
messages:
From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@finexpay.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:05:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Call recap — Finex performance & SLOs

Alex — thanks again for taking the call earlier. Quick recap and a couple of follow-ups so we can size accurately: 

Summary from call:
- Primary use: customer support chat + event-based alerts (low-touch financial alerts) with streaming responses for agent UI.
- Model family you're evaluating: open LLMs (performance comparable to 13B-70B-class models) — you mentioned a couple of fine-tuned variants.
- Target SLOs you stated: p95 latency target for first token (interactive streaming) ~ < 300ms; end-to-end p95 for a typical completion (avg ~600 tokens) ~ < 1200ms.
- Traffic profile (what we heard): steady-state: ~30 RPS (requests/sec) with avg response length ~400–800 tokens; peak bursts up to ~200 RPS with short spikes lasting 1–5 minutes. Concurrency target ~40–75 concurrent sessions during peak.

Quick clarifying questions (so the sizing workbook is accurate):
1) When you say RPS, is that requests/sec measured at the UI (user keystroke -> server) or at completion boundaries? For streaming SLOs we care about time-to-first-token measured at the client's keystroke.
2) Can you confirm average prompt length (tokens) vs average response length (tokens)? I used 150 tokens prompt / 600 tokens response in the attached worksheet as a starting point.
3) Do you require strict ordering for streamed tokens (i.e., must deliver every token as produced), or are you ok with small buffering windows (10–50ms) to improve batching efficiency?

Next steps: I've attached a preliminary throughput workbook (redwood_throughput_workbook_v1.xlsx) and our suggested SLA outline (redwood-sla-draft.pdf). If you can drop the traffic sample (CSV) back in reply or confirm the questions above, I’ll run a quick sizing and propose an initial Dedicated pool (GPU + concurrency) to cover steady-state and peak.

Best,
Neha Kapoor
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
neha.kapoor@redwood.ai
+1 (415) 555-0162

Attachment: redwood_throughput_workbook_v1.xlsx (spreadsheet stub)
Attachment: redwood-sla-draft.pdf (PDF stub)

From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@finexpay.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2026 16:32:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Call recap — Finex performance & SLOs

Neha — thanks for the recap and workbook. A few clarifications from our side: 

- RPS measurement: our frontend measures at the user action boundary (keystroke/send) — so RPS is at request arrival. For streaming we measure time-to-first-token from that boundary, so your first-token SLO phrasing is correct.
- Token averages: confirmed — prompts ~150 tokens (range 60–300), responses average ~600 tokens (range 120–1200) for agent-assist flows.
- Streaming buffer: we prefer minimal buffering to preserve perceived realtime; target buffering <= 50ms. If batching yields significant cost savings we can consider slightly larger windows but prefer <100ms.

I've attached a small traffic sample export (finex_traffic_profile.csv) that shows 24 hours of minute-level RPS and median token counts — it includes a few burst events.

Can you also call out whether prefix/KV caching would help us (we have lots of repeated prompts across agents for templated workflows). We expect a decent hit rate for repeated prefixes.

Happy to take a sizing call next week.

— Alex
Alex Johnson
Head of Platform Engineering, FinexPay
alex.johnson@finexpay.com

Attachment: finex_traffic_profile.csv (CSV stub)

From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@finexpay.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 09:18:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Call recap — Finex performance & SLOs (workbook + initial sizing)

Alex — thanks for the CSV, that helps a lot. I ran the attached workbook with your numbers and sketched an initial sizing. Highlights below (see workbook for line-by-line assumptions):

Assumptions used:
- Avg prompt: 150 tokens, avg response: 600 tokens -> avg payload ~750 tokens per request.
- Steady-state: 30 RPS -> ~22,500 tokens/sec (750 * 30).
- Peak burst: 200 RPS sustained for short windows -> ~150,000 tokens/sec.
- Concurrency: we model token-level concurrency; typical concurrency at peak ~60–80 concurrent sessions.

Preliminary sizing (ballpark):
- Baseline (steady-state): 2 x A100-80GB or 3 x H100 (driverless sizing depends on exact model variant). This presumes streaming-optimized kernels and modest batching.
- Peak (covering bursts to 200 RPS with low buffering): recommend elastic Dedicated autoscale to 6–8 GPUs across the pool with policy to scale based on token/sec and queued requests.

Optimizations to reduce required capacity / cost:
- Prefix/KV caching: with a good hit rate (e.g., 20–30% repeated prefix reuse) we can reduce tokens-in-flight by ~10–25% for your workload — workbook models this.
- Small batching windows (30–50ms) increase GPU throughput for steady-state without materially affecting perceived latency.
- Quantized model variants (int8 or 4-bit with Redwood-tested runtimes) can reduce memory footprint and increase throughput; we included a variant-based estimate in the workbook.

SLO recommendations (draft):
- First-token (streaming) p95: 300ms (measured client->first token).
- Completion p95 (for avg ~600 tokens): 1200ms.
- Availability target: 99.9% for hosted endpoints; for Dedicated we can discuss SLA language — attached draft.

Open items for sizing accuracy:
- Exact model variant (13B vs 70B vs custom FT) — GPU counts vary widely. Please indicate which model you expect to run in production.
- Expected cache hit rate for repeated prefixes.
- Tolerance for small extra buffering (we recommend testing 30–50ms window).

Next steps: Rafael and Marissa — adding you to loop to sanity-check the sizing assumptions. Alex, can we schedule a 30-min call Tuesday or Wednesday next week to walk the workbook and confirm model variant? Once confirmed we can produce an official Dedicated pool recommendation and an estimated monthly cost.

Thanks,
Neha

Attachment: redwood_throughput_workbook_v1.xlsx (updated with assumed numbers)

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael.mendes@redwood.ai>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@finexpay.com>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 11:04:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Call recap — Finex performance & SLOs (internal notes)

Looping in a couple of internal sizing checks. Neha — good start. A few notes from infra/serving perspective:
- If they're running a 70B-class FT model with streaming enabled, the GPU delta is material: plan for the higher end of the autoscale recommendation (6–8 H100s) for peak. 13B-class models are far cheaper (2–4 GPUs).
- For low-buffer streaming (<50ms), we should bias toward lower-latency kernels and higher concurrency rather than long batching windows; that increases GPU count but preserves UX.
- Recommend we include an explicit fallback policy: if Dedicated pool is saturated, route to a slightly smaller, cheaper model family in Hosted mode for best-effort availability (Redwood supports automated fallback).

I'll review the workbook assumptions and add a separate tab with GPU SKU mapping. Neha — I can be on the Tuesday call to discuss tradeoffs.

-Rafael
Rafael Mendes
Head of Solutions, Redwood Inference
rafael.mendes@redwood.ai

From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@finexpay.com>

Date: Sun, 15 Nov 2026 10:12:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Call recap — Finex performance & SLOs

All — thanks for the quick turn. Tuesday 2026-11-17 10:00am PT works for me to review the workbook and model choices. We'll plan to discuss: model variant (we'll confirm whether to go 13B FT or 70B FT), expected cache hit rates (we'll run a quick prefix analysis Monday), and acceptable buffering.

Also, please include a short slide with estimated monthly cost for baseline vs peak capacity in the call notes. If we can get that ahead of the call, we can expedite purchasing approval.

— Alex
